This is a Khmer translation of a Thai-language original: Whayooathdee, Photpeechon, "Jackfruit (2nd edition)", Nonthaburi Province, Thailand: Agriculture Lover's Printing House, 1988. text:
This chapter covers care of the tree around the flowering and early fruit-set stage, with particular attention to the problem of flower and young-fruit drop, which the text identifies as a major cause of reduced yield if not managed. It explains that jackfruit trees typically set far more flowers/young fruitlets than they can support to maturity, and that a proportion of natural drop is normal, but excessive drop — caused by nutrient stress, water stress, poor pollination, pest damage, or overcrowding of fruit on a branch — can significantly reduce the final harvest.

The chapter discusses fruit thinning as a deliberate management practice: removing excess young fruit early (leaving a more limited, well-spaced number of fruit per branch or per tree) so that the remaining fruit receive more of the tree's resources and develop to a larger, better-quality size, rather than allowing the tree to carry an excessive number of small, poorly developed fruit. Guidance is given on roughly how much fruit a healthy branch or tree of a given size can be expected to properly support, and on timing thinning relatively early after fruit set, before the tree has invested heavily in fruit that will ultimately be removed.

The chapter also addresses supplementary care during this stage: maintaining adequate but not excessive soil moisture (linking back to the water-requirements chapter, since both drought stress and sudden waterlogging around this stage are associated with increased fruit drop and cracking), and providing balanced fertilization timed to support flower and fruit development rather than excessive vegetative growth, which the text notes can come at the expense of fruiting if nitrogen is over-applied relative to phosphorus and potassium at this stage.
